content: At Nash University in Australia, systematic reviews of studies were conducted for each syndrome to identify research comparing different approaches and their effects on significant outcomes. When such studies were unavailable, additional reviews were performed to assess the prevalence of suspected sexually transmitted infections (STIs) and the accuracy of various syndromic approaches, including risk assessment, history-taking, clinical signs, and diagnostic tests. Comprehensive searches for systematic reviews, randomized controlled trials, and non-randomized studies were conducted up to September 2019. Additional searches were also performed to identify studies on patient values, preferences, acceptability, feasibility, equity, and resource use, such as cost-effectiveness studies. The systematic review process was conducted in duplicate, and statistical pooling of results was performed when feasible. Reviews on the treatment of suspected STIs, including chlamydia, gonorrhea, syphilis, and herpes, were previously conducted for WHO treatment guidelines and provided data on treatment outcomes. When data on the effects of interventions on important outcomes were unavailable, these effects were calculated using diagnostic test accuracy data from studies. The number of true positives, true negatives, false positives, and false negatives was calculated based on the sensitivity, specificity, and prevalence of the STI in symptomatic populations. These findings were discussed with the Guideline Development Group to evaluate the consequences of diagnostic errors, such as false negatives, on patients and health systems. For the syndromic management of vaginal discharge, a static model using Excel was developed to simulate various management strategies for identifying and treating vaginal and cervical infections. This model built upon previous WHO work to create a comprehensive and flexible tool capable of simulating different patient management flowcharts based on syndromic management, existing diagnostic procedures, and tests (e.g., speculum examination and Gram stain) in diverse settings. The strategies included combinations of risk assessment, speculum examination, microscopy, and rapid point-of-care diagnostic tests, alongside WHO-recommended syndromic management approaches. Costs and effects were calculated based on STI prevalence, incorporating direct costs of managing vaginal discharge (e.g., test and treatment costs) and optional costs of long-term consequences (e.g., pelvic inflammatory disease, ectopic pregnancy, infertility) and partner management. Due to limited evidence on the direct cost of overtreatment and its impact on antimicrobial resistance, an antimicrobial resistance externality tax was included. This tax accounted for the current and future burden of antimicrobial resistance, including costs of treating resistant infections, increased morbidity and mortality, and the development of new drugs. Evidence tables were created to facilitate decision-making for recommendations, summarizing diagnostic accuracy, benefits, harms, certainty of evidence, patient values, costs, resources, feasibility, equity, and acceptability. The certainty of evidence was assessed using the GRADE system, considering factors such as risk of bias, inconsistency, indirectness, imprecision, publication bias, effect size, dose-response, and confounding. Based on these criteria, evidence certainty was categorized as very low, low, moderate, or high. The STI Guideline Development Group reviewed the evidence-to-decision tables and evidence summaries during virtual meetings held from September 28 to October 2, 2020. Decisions on whether to make strong or conditional recommendations for or against an approach were made by consensus, with no disagreements requiring voting. Recommendations and evidence-to-decision tables were finalized electronically via email. According to the GRADE approach, strong recommendations were presented as recommendations, while conditional recommendations were presented as suggestions. Good practice statements were issued when guidance was deemed necessary without requiring a literature review, as the balance of consequences was unequivocal. The External Review Group approved the methods and agreed with the recommendations made by the Guideline Development Group. Managing conflicts of interest was a priority throughout the guideline development process. WHO guidelines for declaring interests were implemented, and all members of the Guideline Development Group and External Review Group disclosed their interests before assuming their roles. These declarations were summarized as per WHO Guidelines Review Committee recommendations. Five members declared interests, and after analysis, one member with a significant non-commercial research grant and minor commercial interest was allowed partial participation. Two members with consultancy roles unrelated to the guidelines were allowed full participation, as were two members with minimal or past pharmaceutical support. The objectives of comprehensive STI case management include providing treatment, achieving cure, reducing infectiousness, minimizing complications, and preventing future risk-taking behaviors. This involves offering medical and sexual history-taking, accurate diagnosis (syndromic or test-based), effective treatment, health education, counseling, advice on treatment compliance, promotion or provision of condoms and preventive interventions (e.g., vaccines, PrEP, male circumcision), partner notification, and clinical follow-up. Effective case management requires not only antimicrobial therapy but also comprehensive care for the reproductive health of the patient and their partners. For adolescents, services must be accessible, non-judgmental, and user-friendly to encourage engagement at a critical developmental stage. To achieve these objectives, high-quality STI care must be available at the first point of contact with the healthcare system. Integrated care should be offered at primary healthcare facilities to reduce stigma and promote service use. This requires appropriate training for healthcare providers and equipping facilities with necessary commodities and equipment. During consultations, healthcare providers must create a conducive environment for patients to discuss STI symptoms freely. This includes ensuring privacy, providing private examination facilities with good lighting, and using examination gloves. History-taking, particularly sexual history, is crucial for assessing the likelihood of STI infection. Providers should adopt a non-judgmental approach to make patients comfortable discussing intimate issues. Risk assessment should consider factors such as recent unprotected sexual contact, partner STI status, and demographic or behavioral risk factors. Women presenting with abnormal vaginal discharge should undergo thorough medical and sexual history-taking and physical examination, ideally with a speculum to view the cervix. External genital examination is preferable to no examination at all. Physical examination of patients with STI-related symptoms should focus on the anogenital area while also assessing for other STI manifestations, such as lymphadenopathy, skin rashes, and abdominal abnormalities. Examinations should be conducted with patient consent and, where possible, in the presence of a chaperone. Findings should be recorded to complement the history and guide management using appropriate flowcharts.
